full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This Rule was obtained by the preemptor upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and order dated 31-03-99 passed by Additional District Judge, Fifth Court at Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 223 of 1996 affirming those dated 12-10-96 passed by Subordinate Judge, Fourth Court at Dhaka in Preemption Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1992 which disallowed the prayer for preemption. 

 2. The preemptor made an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, in brief, the Act against the opposite parties for preemption of the transfer of 0.0907 acre of land of SA plot No. 54 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 48/1 out of CS plot No. 139 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 2 by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No.1. His case, in short, is that said khatian No. 2 consisted of 5 plots of which CS plot No.139 comprised of 3.49 acre of land. Owners of other plots got settlements from the Bhowal Raj Court of Wards Estate by opening separate holdings. The CS plot No. 139 was joint and still remained joint and other owners of other four plots were never co-sharers in this plot. 

 3. Lal Mahmud, Waz Mahmud, Shukur Mahmud and Noor Mahmud took settlement of 2.36 acres from said Court of Wards Estate and the rest 1.13 acre was given settlement to Ibrahim and his brother Wasimuddin. Said Lal Mahmud and three others transferred their land to Nishi Kanta Shome, Rebati Mohan Shome and Amrita Lal Shome. Then, one Golam Mowla purchased the said land from them by deed No. 5935 dated 27-08-51 and deed No. 6755 dated 27-09-51 and became owner in possession. Similarly, Ibrahim and his brother transferred their land to one Charu Bala. Thereafter, the land was sold in auction for arrears of rents and one Jamsher Ali purchased said land measuring 1.13 acre in the auction. The auction was confirmed on 23-12-49 and possession was delivered to him on 31-01-50. 

 6. Haji Tarikullah instituted Partition Suit No. 43 of 1993 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka for partition. Father of the preemptor is defendant No.3 in the suit. The parents of the preemptor jointly prayed for a 'Saham' in respect of their purchased land of 0.63 acre. The suit was on 15-12-54 decreed in the preliminary form the suit was then transferred to the Fourth Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka and was re-numbered as Partition Suit No. 584 of 1993. The suit is still pending for final decree. Further case of the preemptor is that CS plot No. 139 was never partitioned by metes and bound and, as such, he is still a co-sharer in said land and is therefore entitled to pre-empt. Having come to know about the transfer of the case land by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1, the application was filed on making the statutory deposit. 

 11. The learned Subordinate Judge found the preemptor not a co-sharer in the land and accordingly, disallowed the application. On appeal therefrom at the instance .of the preemptor, the learned Additional District Judge hearing the same was also pleased to affirm the decision of the trial Court, and dismissed the appeal by impugned judgment and order. 

 12. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner read section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 and submits that the preemptor is still a co-sharer in the land of CS plot No. 139 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 2 and the Courts below erred in law in disallowing preemption on the view that the preemptor is not a co-sharer in land. Elaborating, he submits that CS plot 139 was never partitioned by metes and bound and until a final decree in the Partition Suit is passed the preemptor must be held to be a co-sharer in said land. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Muhammad Muzaffar Khan vs Muhammad Yusuf Khan, 11 DLR (SC) 78, SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 230 and Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md Abdul Karim and others, 52 DLR (AD) 41. 

 13. Opposing the Rule, Mr. Md Ismail, learned Counsel for the purchaser, opposite party No. 1 submits that the land measuring 3.49 as was recorded as CS plot in 1917-18 in the Cadastral survey was split up in numerous plots under various khatians during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in 1964 and the persons including the preemptor have been exclusively possessing their respective land according to such record of rights. The parents of the preemptor were in exclusive possession in their 0.63 acre of land which was recorded as SA plot No. 92 under SA khatian No. 73 Exhibit 'Ka' while opposite party No. 2 was in exclusive possession in plot No. 54 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 4811. The preemptor is therefore not a co-sharer in the land transferred by the kabala Exhibit No. 8. He accordingly, submits that the learned Additional District Judge did not commit any error in affirming the order of the trial Court in disallowing preemption. He also submits that everyone of purchasers of land of said CS plot No. 139 including the parents of the preemptor got their names mutated and in view of provisions of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the parents of the preemptor ceased to be co-sharer in said land. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Haladar Dutta vs Abdul Rob Chowdhury, 36 DLR 193 and Md Khairullah vs Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 338. 

 14. Only question facing us is whether the learned Additional District Judge is well founded in affirming the decision of the trial Court in disallowing the application for preemption. More precisely, the issue raised for our decision is whether the preemptor is a co-sharer in the land transferred by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1 by a sale deed No. 1677 dated 30-06-91, Exhibit No.8 within the meaning of section 24 of the Act, 1949. 

 Upon such finding, the Supreme Court of Pakistan restored the decision of first two Courts allowing preemption. What Khata, khasras, kanals etc, means, we could not ascertain. Nor we could ascertain the land law in Peshawar at the time. Unlike our land tenure, the land laws there, particularly, in the then West Pakistan was tilted a bit to big land holdings, Besides, unless the law for preemption in Peshawar is not in pari-materia with our law, i.e. the Act, 1949, in brief, the Act, 1949, it is very difficult for us to follow the opinion of the Pakistan Supreme Court. Moreover, if we take Khata meaning a tenancy or holding, the above view of the Supreme Court of Pakistan will be of no help because sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have provided procedure for amalgamation and subdivision of a tenancy or holding, and after a valid subdivision of a holding and distribution of the rents, preemption at the instance of a co-sharer of the former joint holding is not maintainable. 

 17. SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 230 arose out of an application under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The case land appertained to a permanent tenure recorded in CS Khatian No. 214 in the names of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani. Akshoy instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 for partition and by the decree passed, Akshoy got one-third share while Rangubala got the rest two-third. One Nafisa Khatun purchased the entire share of Akshoy by a registered sale deed dated 19-07-52 while Rangubala settled her share of two-third for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 with Ayesha Khatun, respondent No. 2. Then, Nafisa Khatun sold her share to respondent No. 1 by a registered deed of sale dated 18-04-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered deed of sale dated 10- 09-73. Against this sale, respondent No.1 filed the application for preemption, which was allowed by the trial Court. Against the order, appellant's appeal and revision failed. But the Appellate Division set aside the order and dismissed the application for preemption. But, we find, on different reasons. 

 "Secondly, a Full Bench of the High Court in the case of 'Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury vs Rezia Begum'; 16 DLR 77 examined this question and by majority decision held that these two terms, 'Non-Agricultural land' and 'holding', are synonymous carrying the same meaning, Since this question is not necessary for disposal of the instant appeal, I would refrain from expressing any opinion as to the correctness of the decision of the High Court in that case." 

 "In this case also by effecting partition on the basis of a decree of the Civil Court the co- sharers, namely, Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Chouwdhurani possessed separately the land in their respective share, but the tenancy with the jama of Rs 10 was not divided or split up." 

 "Amalgamation of tenancies made in Miscellaneous Case No. 89/72-73 under sections 116 and 117(1)(a) was given effect by amending khatian No. 14 after excluding plot No. 108 therefrom and revenue was collected on the basis of the new khatian No. 18. Prima facie the order was a valid one; its validity could not be challenged for a collateral purpose, that is, in a proceeding of preemption. The Civil Court while dealing with altogether a different matter cannot ignore the order passed by a competent Revenue Officer under section 117 of the Act." 

 23. Ratio decidendi in the above decisions is that a decree of the Court in a partition suit brings separation and division in the joint possession and enjoyment of land. But such decree does not ipso facto result in the splitting of holding along with the jama till such subdivision of the holding and distribution of the rents takes place in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act or the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the case may be. Such division of the land may also be brought about by an amicable partition among the co-sharers in such land. But the main submission of Mr. Islam is that the total area of land in a plot as was plotted in the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must to be taken as an undivided unit. If such land was recorded in the names of more than one person, all such persons and/or their successors-in-interest must be held to be co-sharers in such plot till the land is partitioned by a decree of the Court or by amicable partition among such co-sharers. Even any sub-division of such CS plot and/or the holding to which such plot appertained in subsequent survey, say, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 will not result in the termination of co-sharer ship in such land and thereby, taking away the right of preemption under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The argument appears to be unique in the sense that it was never argued since the Act came into force in 1949. We are unable to accept such interpretation of the law. 

 29. In the facts and circumstances of the case, and on the above principles, we could not find any reason to differ from the concurrent conclusion of the Courts below that the preemptor ceased to be a co-sharer in the land in question and, as such, his application for preemption was rightly found to be not maintainable. No failure of justice has occasioned by the decision. 

 30. In the result, the Rule is discharged with costs. Impugned judgment and order affirming the order of the trial Court in disallowing the application for preemption are confirmed. Order of stay as granted at the time of issue of the Rule is hereby recalled and vacated.
